questions.question: Why is ordinary autoregressive generation slow for a long response?
options: The tokenizer must rebuild its vocabulary at every step
Each generated token waits for the previous one
The verifier cannot read multiple tokens in one pass
The model discards every hidden state after each token
questions.explanation: Autoregressive decoding feeds each sampled token back as the next step’s context, so token t+1 cannot be generated until token t is known. A verifier can evaluate a batch of draft candidates together, but ordinary generation lacks those candidates.

questions.question: A draft proposes token d with probability p(d), and the verifier assigns q(d). What is its acceptance probability?
options: q(d) − p(d), without normalization
p(d) + q(d), capped at one
min(1, p(d) / q(d))
min(1, q(d) / p(d))
questions.explanation: The algorithm accepts a draft with probability min(1, q(d)/p(d)): if the verifier assigns at least as much probability as the draft, it accepts surely; otherwise it accepts in proportion to q/p. Reversing the ratio favors tokens the verifier considers less likely.

questions.question: When the verifier rejects a draft token, what distribution supplies the replacement token?
options: The draft distribution p without modification
The verifier distribution q minus its maximum
The normalized positive part of q minus p
A uniform distribution across the vocabulary
questions.explanation: On rejection, clamp each q−p entry below zero to zero, then normalize the remaining mass. This residual corrects for the draft probability already accounted for; sampling directly from p would leave the verifier’s desired distribution uncorrected.

questions.question: If every one of N draft tokens is accepted, what does the algorithm sample next?
options: The residual distribution supplies one extra bonus token
A bonus token sampled from the draft model distribution
The last draft token is repeated after full acceptance
One bonus token from the verifier’s next-step distribution
questions.explanation: Once all N proposals pass, sample the next-position bonus token from the verifier’s distribution q. Using the draft model for that token would introduce its distribution instead of continuing from the verifier.

questions.question: A creative high-temperature workload has a draft model with poor agreement with the verifier. What should the team expect?
options: Identical acceptance regardless of draft quality
Lower acceptance and a smaller speedup
No change because the verifier runs once
Higher acceptance because sampling is diverse
questions.explanation: Speculative speedup depends on how many draft tokens the verifier accepts. High-temperature sampling and a poor draft-verifier match reduce acceptance, so fewer tokens are produced per verifier call; diverse sampling does not improve agreement.

questions.question: The verifier tentatively appended five draft tokens. After accepting tokens 1–2 and rejecting token 3, what should production code do?
options: Clear the entire cache and restart the whole request
Commit the rejected token and regenerate only its logits
Roll back to the accepted prefix and discard later drafts
Keep all five entries and continue with the sixth draft
questions.explanation: After draft tokens 1–2 are accepted and token 3 fails, keep the prefix through token 2 and discard tentative cache entries for token 3 and later drafts. Then append the residual replacement; retaining rejected entries would corrupt the next prefix.
